## Summary

Physical AI chipmaker Sima.ai has secured $150 million in Series C funding, valuing the company at $1.45 billion, bringing total investment to $500 million. The seven-year-old startup is poised to power the booming physical AI market, including drones, autonomous vehicles, and various robots. Sima.ai claims its chips outperform Nvidia's Jetson Orin, offering twice the performance at one-fifth the power, making them ideal for production systems. Their second-gen Modalix chip is in production, with a third generation targeting double Nvidia Thor's performance at 60 watts by 2028. The company also emphasizes its "Palette Neat" agentic software, designed to simplify application development and ease migration from Nvidia platforms, supporting ROS 2 and concurrent VLM operation. Sima.ai anticipates significant growth as the robotics industry shifts from training to operational deployment.

Physical AI chipmaker SiMa.ai announced today that it has raised a $150 million Series C at a $1.45 billion valuation, bringing its total funding to $500 million.

Getty Images

“It’s a $5 trillion Nvidia and then it’s us,” Sima.ai founder and CEO Krishna Rangasayee told me last week. “My world is very simple.”

Sima.ai is a physical AI chipmaker, and now is a very good time to be in physical AI. The space is exploding right now with hundreds of billions of dollars in investment. Haomiao Huang, founding partner at Matter Venture Partners, explained why in a recent podcast recording that I have yet to publish, saying that “if AI is gonna eat the world, hardware will be its teeth.”

The news today is that Sima.ai has raised a $150 million Series C at a $1.45 billion valuation, bringing its total funding to $500 million. The story behind the story is that the 200-employee seven-year-old startup is just now hitting an inflection curve where its chips will power medium-sized-to-large drones (growth industry), smart-ish to near or full self-driving cars (growth industry) and all kinds of robots from quadrupeds to humanoids (also a growth industry).

And, the company says, its chips will do more than Nvidia for less cost using less power and generating less waste heat, because its chips are optimized for physical AI, not AI inference. (That’s where Nvidia reigns supreme for now, but it’s only a fraction of what a robot needs in its compute stack.)

“Our primary competition has been Jetson Orin class of products,” Rangasayee says, referencing Nvidia’s family of chips and kits for next-generation robots that offer up to 275 trillion operations per second of performance. “And so we are typically twice the performance of Nvidia on tokens per second or frames per second, but we are 1/5th the power.”

A robotics CEO once told me that compute in a humanoid robot can demand up to 40% of the robot’s power draw, so that’s fairly significant.

Of course, these are Sima.ai’s numbers, not independent benchmarks. But they speak to a real problem. Nvidia’s newer Jetson Thor platform is powerful, and plenty of the humanoid robot companies I talk to use it. It’s also expensive, and it’s power-hungry.

Rangasayee has Nvidia and its $5 trillion valuation squarely in his sights:

“Nvidia is wonderful for prototyping, but you want to really build a production worthy system,” Rangasayee says. “Humanoid or otherwise, $3,500 to $5,000 is not the economic footprint you want for compute, number one. Number two, it’s 130 watts and that is not the footprint you want for a production worthy scale system.”

Shots fired.

Rangasayee started Sima.ai nearly a decade ago when, as he puts it, “it was really cool to start a cloud AI company.” Instead, however, he chose to do “the wonky, difficult bit and actually build a company for physical AI.” He’s spent 35-odd years building compute in various forms for companies like Xilinx, AI chip startup Groq and Cypress Semiconductor after taking a masters in electrical engineering. It’s a resume built on programmable chips that power everything from cars to cell towers, which is not far from a pretty good job description for physical AI.

Now he’s pairing the chips that will power physical AI with the agentic AI software that will help us extract their full power orders of magnitude faster than we could in years past.

Sima.ai’s second-generation chip, Modalix, is built on TSMC’s 6 nanometer process and is in production now. The Series C will fund the third generation, which Rangasayee says will deliver twice the performance of Thor at just 60 watts. The company says its next-generation hardware will hit 1,000 dense TOPS and ship in the first half of 2028 as IP, chiplets and full SoCs.

But the software is just as important.

“If you want to build a great chip company, you need to be an awesome software company,” Rangasayee says, conceding that this is the thing Nvidia has done better than anyone else, building a competitive moat with CUDA: AI software that integrates tightly with its chips and development kits.

A core problem: AI models change fast, while chips change slow. The industry has gone from LLMs to VLMs to VLAs to world foundation models in a remarkably short period of time, but silicon designed three years ago has to run all of it.

“AI is moving at a monthly, if not bimonthly cadence in terms of architectures and evolution, but silicon churn is once every three years,” he says. “How do you keep the two worlds congruent or concurrent? It’s a massive software problem in the industry.”

SiMa.ai’s answer is Palette Neat, which the company calls the industry’s first agentic software environment for physical AI. The pitch: robot makers don’t have to understand the architecture at all. They simply describe their dataset and their constraints on throughput, latency, power and accuracy, and the system builds the application. Think vibe coding for robots.

“Our customers unanimously want the AI experience, but not the learning curve,” Rangasayee told me. “They really don’t want to know my architecture. They don’t want to know my software. They just want to be able to push a button and it works.”

The company is also making it easy to leave Nvidia. Nvidia sells system-on-module boards, not just bare chips, so Sima.ai built a replacement.

“Just remove the Nvidia SOM, slide in the SiMa SOM,” Rangasayee says. “It’s pin-to-pin compatible, and it’s production qualified.”

On the software side, Sima.ai has built agentic skills and libraries so that customers can “watch an Nvidia codebase migrate and become a Sima codebase,” he says, whether it was optimized for CUDA or TensorRT. The company is currently touring drone makers with a simple offer: bring your drone stack, and SiMa.ai will port it live. In other words: during the meeting. In, essentially, real time.

“What even I have held as a notion is it takes nine months to build any complicated application in physical AI,” Rangasayee says. “We are changing that to a day.”

That’s a huge claim, and a single day for a production-grade robotics application is probably going to depend a lot on how you define “application.” But it’s in line with what’s happening across AI-assisted engineering right now. Nvidia-backed General Robotics recently told me that AI [wrote 80% of its code](https://www.forbes.com/sites/johnkoetsier/2026/09/09/nvidia-backed-robot-platform-says-ai-wrote-80-of-its-code-cuts-robot-training-time-99/) and cuts robot training time by 99%. Anyone who’s done serious vibe coding over the past year knows the speedups are real, even if the results aren’t always perfect.

Rangasayee says customers tend to walk in skeptical.

“I love the skepticism my customers come in with and then they walk out,” he says. “So I ask them, how did it feel? They’re like, it worked.”

There’s one more technical capability that caught my eye. Most robots I see run multiple layers of intelligence: low-level control, something like ROS for operating the robot, higher-level reasoning for planning tasks, LLMs for communications, and fleet-level intelligence on top. Sima.ai supports ROS 2 natively and says it can run several vision-language models at the same time on a single chip.

“We are the only company that can concurrently run multiple VLMs together,” Rangasayee says.

Sima.ai says revenue quadrupled from 2024 to 2025, and its customer and partner list includes Bosch, Emerson, Micron, Synopsys, TRUMPF, STIGA, Kontron and Intrinsic. That last one is interesting, given that Google’s Intrinsic just [open-sourced Intrinsic Core](https://www.forbes.com/sites/johnkoetsier/2026/09/22/google-is-giving-away-the-android-of-robotics/).

Sima.ai’s own software is open source on GitHub as well.

As for humanoids specifically, Rangasayee expects real volume to start showing up in 2028, which lines up with Sima.ai’s next-generation hardware. And he thinks the industry is about to repeat the data center’s history. Ten years ago, he says, training was 90% of data center revenue. Now it’s flipped to delivering AI services … answering our questions, essentially.

“We have the same problem now in robotics,” he says. “Gradually, it’s going to go 10-90 the other way around.”

In other words: today everyone’s obsessed with training robots. Soon, the money will be in running them.

The other obsession in robotics right now is form factor, and whether robots really need to be humanoid to win, or quadruped, wheeled or legged, or any other form factor. Rangasayee isn’t picking sides.

“This debate of do you need a humanoid factor to win will go on for 20 years,” he says. “Why argue with gravity?”

Sima.ai will sell chips to all of them.
